title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA): The Ophthalmic Emergency + Temporal Artery Biopsy...
summary: Giant Cell Arteritis (Horton's Disease) is a systemic granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large-sized arteries. In ophthalmology, it represents a 'code red' emergency due to its propensity for sudden, irreversible bilateral vision loss via Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION). An exhaustive guide to the diagnostic accuracy of temporal artery biopsy (TAB) and ultrasound in Giant Cell Arteritis, featuring findings from the landmark TABUL study. This layout details sensitivity, specificity, clinical indications, and the essential risks required for informed patient consent. Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy (AION) is a major cause of acute vision loss in patients over 50. This guide provides an exhaustive breakdown of diagnostic criteria, emergency management for Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), and the surgical approach for temporal artery biopsy. A-AION is an ophthalmic emergency secondary to Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), characterized by acute, painless, altitudinal visual field loss. Rapid recognition is essential to prevent bilateral blindness and systemic complications.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is a chronic vasculitis of large and medium-sized vessels, primarily involving the extracranial branches of the carotid artery. It is the most common primary systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. The ophthalmic hallmark is Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (A-AION), caused by occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries (SPCAs).

branches: Activation of adventitial dendritic cells via Toll-like receptors
Recruitment of CD4+ T-cells (Th1 and Th17 pathways)
Macrophage fusion into Multinucleated Giant Cells
Destruction of the Internal Elastic Lamina

rows: New onset or new type of localized pain in the head
Tenderness to palpation or decreased pulsation
Vasculitis with mononuclear cell infiltration or granulomatous inflammation

sections.title: Systemic Clinical Features
content: New-onset localized headache (often temporal)
Jaw Claudication (High specificity for GCA)
Scalp tenderness (pain when brushing hair)
Polymyalgia Rheumatica (stiffness in hips/shoulders)
Constitutional: Fever, weight loss, anorexia, malaise
Carotidynia or limb claudication

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations
content: Amaurosis Fugax: Transient vision loss (Warning sign!)
A-AION: Sudden, profound, painless vision loss
CRAO: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
Cilio-retinal Artery Occlusion (Pathognomonic if combined with A-AION)
Diplopia: Due to cranial nerve palsies or EOM ischemia
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (rare)

sections.title: EMERGENCY: Red Flags
content: Sudden vision loss in a patient >50 years old
New-onset headache with jaw claudication
Chalky-white disc edema on fundoscopy
Diplopia in an elderly patient with constitutional symptoms
Delayed choroidal filling on Fluorescein Angiography

sections.title: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) Protocol
content: Step 1: Perform within 1-2 weeks of starting steroids
Step 2: Obtain 2-3 cm length to minimize 'skip lesion' errors
Step 3: Incise skin over the frontal branch of the temporal artery
Step 4: Careful dissection to preserve facial nerve branches
Step 5: Ligation and excision of the segment
Step 6: Histopathological exam for Giant Cells and Intimal thickening

sections.title: The 'Halo Sign' on Ultrasound
sections.content: Color Doppler Ultrasound of the temporal arteries is an increasingly used non-invasive tool. A positive 'Halo Sign'—a hypoechoic area around the arterial lumen representing vessel wall edema—has high specificity. If bilateral halos are seen, sensitivity approaches 85%.

sections.title: Acute Management Protocol
content: 1. Immediate Start: DO NOT wait for biopsy if suspicion is high.
2. Vision Loss Present: IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day) for 3 days.
3. Oral Bridge: Transition to Oral Prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (Max 60-80mg).
4. Tapering: Very slow taper (over 12-18 months) based on CRP/ESR and symptoms.
5. Steroid Sparing: Consider Tocilizumab (Actemra) - IL-6 Receptor Antagonist.
6. Protection: Add PPI, Calcium/Vitamin D, and Bisphosphonates for bone health.

content.explanation: S: Scalp tenderness, T: Temporal headache, A: Amaurosis fugax, I: Ischemic optic neuropathy, R: Rheumatism (PMR symptoms)

sections.title: Recent Advances: GiACTA Trial
content: Tocilizumab (anti-IL-6) is FDA approved for GCA.
Proven to increase sustained remission rates.
Significantly reduces cumulative steroid dose.
Administered as weekly or bi-weekly subcutaneous injections.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Bilateral blindness: Risk is highest in the first 24-48 hours without treatment.
Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm: Late complication (occur in up to 18%).
Stroke: From vertebrobasilar involvement.
Steroid-induced: Diabetes, Osteoporosis, Glaucoma, Cataract.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Normal ESR does NOT rule out GCA (Occurs in ~15-20% of biopsy-proven cases).
Always check CRP; the combination of ESR and CRP has 97% sensitivity.
If vision is lost in one eye, there is a 50-90% chance of the second eye being affected within days.
Biopsy remains the gold standard but should never delay treatment.

sections.title: The TABUL Study Findings
content: The TABUL study found that for diagnosing GCA, clinical judgement (clinician’s assessment at 2wk) combined with a TAB showed sensitivity and specificity of 91% and 81%, respectively.
Clinical judgement combined with duplex US showed sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 77%, respectively.
The cost-effectiveness was found in favour of US.
Reference: See Table 16.6 and Box 16.4.

sections.content: Superficial TAB remains highly specific for the diagnosis of GCA (see E Arteritic AION and giant cell arteritis, pp. 744–6). Temporal artery biopsy 749.

sections.title: Surgical Risks & Complications
content: Visible scarring (particularly if incision is pretrichial and not parallel to Langer’s lines).
Haematoma.
Wound infection.
Scalp or skin necrosis.
Facial nerve injury, with variable recovery (particularly if pretrichial incision).
Biopsy does not include the temporal artery (up to 1.25% of specimens in one report were vein or peripheral nerve).
Cerebral infarction (rare; possibly related to collateral blood flow to the brain from the superficial temporal artery).

sections.title: AION: Epidemiology & Vascular Supply
sections.content: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is a significant cause of acute visual loss in the elderly population, affecting up to 10/ 100,000/ y of those over 50y. In 5– 10%, the aetiology is arteritic, in which the majority of these are caused by GCA, and in 90– 95%, the aetiology is non- arteritic (see Table 16.5). The vascular supply to the anterior optic nerve is from the short posterior ciliary artery and the choroidal circulation.

rows: Major: GCA. Minor: Churg– Strauss, PAN, GPA, RA, Relapsing polychondritis, Other connective tissue disorders (e.g. SLE)

Major: Hypertension, Diabetes, Disc morphology ‘disc at risk’. Minor: Smoking, Hyperlipidaemia, Acute hypotension, Anaemia, Obstructive sleep apnoea, Optic disc drusen, Cataract surgery, Non- ocular surgery (e.g. cardiac, spinal), Drugs (e.g. amiodarone, erectile dysfunction drugs), Radiation- induced optic neuropathy

sections.title: Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) Essentials
content: GCA or temporal arteritis is an ophthalmic emergency.
Requires immediate assessment and systemic corticosteroid treatment.
Mean onset is 70y; rare before 50y.
Commonly occurs in Caucasians; 3x more likely in ♀.
Pathology: Short posterior ciliary artery vasculitis leads to ischaemic necrosis of the optic nerve head.
Clinical judgement is required due to disease heterogeneity.

sections.title: GCA Clinical Features
content: Sudden dVA (<6/ 60 in 76%).
New- onset headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, night sweats, myalgia (association with PMR).
Warning episode: Transient dVA (short obscurations or longer amaurosis fugax- like episodes).
Signs: RAPD, swollen disc (typically pale; rarely segmental) ± peripapillary haemorrhages and CWS.
Abnormal temporal arteries: Thickened, tender, non- pulsatile.
Associations: CRAO, BRAO, cilioretinal artery occlusion; III, IV, VIn palsy.

content.explanation: 3+ criteria = 93.5% sensitivity/91.2% specificity: 1. Age ≥50y. 2. New onset localized headache. 3. Temporal artery tenderness or dpulse. 4. ESR ≥50mm/ h (Westerngren). 5. Arterial biopsy showing necrotizing arteritis with mononuclear cell infiltrates or granulomatous process with multinuclear giant cells.

sections.title: Investigations Strategy
content: 1. Immediate Bloods: ESR, CRP, FBC (iESR, iCRP, and iPlt support GCA).
2. Prompt TAB: Recommended length ≥2cm, no <1cm. Aim within 1wk (positive up to 2– 6wk post-treatment).
3. Additional: U+E, LFTs, CXR, and urinalysis.
4. Long term: 2- yearly CXR for aneurysm detection (suspected large-vessel GCA).

sections.title: Diagnostic Imaging & Specialized Tests
content: Duplex US: Hypoechoic ‘halo’ (vessel wall oedema) + stenosis/occlusion. User-dependent; positive >2wk post-steroids.
Fluoro- deoxyglucose PET: Assessing disease activity/extent, especially in large-vessel vasculitis.
High- resolution MRI: Superficial cranial/extracranial arteries (not routinely performed).

sections.title: Emergency Treatment Protocol
content: 1. Immediate systemic corticosteroids: e.g. 1g IVMP 1×/ d for 1– 3d.
2. Oral Follow-up: PO prednisolone 1– 2mg/ kg 1×/ d.
3. Patient Counseling: Mandatory explanation of side effects (gastric/bone protection required).
4. Titration: Once controlled, titrate by symptoms and markers (CRP responds faster than ESR).
5. Specialist Referral: Seek rheumatologist if comorbidities complicate therapy.
6. Emerging Agents: Tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) inducing sustained remission at 1yr. Leflunomide under investigation.

sections.title: Management of Negative TAB
sections.content: If there is a typical clinical/laboratory picture and positive steroid response despite negative TAB, manage as GCA. If history and markers are atypical with negative TAB, consider alternative diagnoses and specialist referral. Steroids can be rapidly tapered within 2wk.

sections.title: Surgical Approach: Superficial TAB (Box 16.3)
content: Preoperative: Choose side of visual loss/abnormality. Map artery by palpation or US Doppler. Mark skin. Hair removal.
Procedure - Cleaning & LA: Clean skin. Infiltrate LA (27G). Adrenaline optional (helps haemostasis/visualization).
Procedure - Incision: Parallel to Langer's lines. Blunt dissection (do not breach superficial temporalis fascia).
Procedure - Ligation: Tie 4- 0 silk/Vicryl twice at distal/proximal ends. Pass needle backwards or double suture without needle. Ligate local tributaries.
Procedure - Specimen Care: Do not crush by regrasping specimen. Maximize biopsy length.
Procedure - Closure: Subcutaneous (5- 0 interrupted Vicryl). Skin (running 6- 0 Vicryl subcuticular).
Post-operative: Compression bandage for 24h. Optional antibiotic ointment for 3– 4d.

sections.title: Definition & Epidemiology
sections.content: A-AION is an ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head due to occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs), typically caused by Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA). It is rare under age 50; incidence increases sharply with age, peaking between 70–80. Prevalence is approximately 15–25 per 100,000 in those over 50 years old.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: The Classic 5-Point Check
content: Sudden, painless loss of vision
Altitudinal visual field defect (most common)
Afferent pupillary defect (APD) present
Chalky-white, swollen optic disc
Peripapillary splinter hemorrhages

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral Criteria
content: Jaw claudication
Scalp tenderness
New-onset temporal headache
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) symptoms
Unilateral vision loss in patient > 60y

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Algorithm
content: Step 1: Immediate ESR (>50-100 mm/hr) and CRP (>10 mg/L) labs.
Step 2: Start high-dose systemic steroids (e.g., IV Methylprednisolone 1g daily for 3 days) BEFORE biopsy.
Step 3: Perform Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) within 1-2 weeks; minimum 2cm length to avoid skip lesions.
Step 4: Ultrasound (USG) of temporal arteries (Halo sign).

rows: Usually associated with disc-at-risk, DM, HTN; no systemic GCA signs
Cherry-red spot, pale retina, no optic disc swelling
High IOP, cup-disc ratio changes, classic arcuate defects
Pain on eye movement, young age, central scotoma

content.explanation: Temporal headache, Jaw claudication, Altered ESR/CRP, Polymyalgia rheumatica, Scalp tenderness.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Normal ESR does not rule out GCA (up to 20% of biopsy-proven cases). CRP is often more sensitive.
Temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard; continue steroids regardless of initial biopsy results if clinical suspicion remains high.
Always inquire about constitutional symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, fatigue.
The 'Halo sign' on temporal artery ultrasound has high specificity but operator-dependent sensitivity.
